solo.title: What is data collection?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova

Where the previous chapter described curated datasets, this chapter focuses on which sources to trust, which instruments to use, and how sampling choices shape what later analysts can claim.

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Data Architect)
solo.title: Why collection design matters

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Collection quality constrains everything that follows. Analysis cannot recover information that was never measured, and biased samples or inconsistent instruments can produce models that look accurate on paper yet fail for underrepresented groups. When protocols are designed well, decisions rest on observed evidence, avoidable measurement error shrinks, and later estimates gain precision—but only after the hard design work of choosing sources, methods, automation level, and samples that match the question.

solo.title: Real-time data

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Real-time data are collected and made available with minimal delay, often through IoT sensors, streaming APIs, or social and analytics feeds. Such feeds usually produce dynamic datasets: records keep arriving, so latency, ordering, and retention become first-class design constraints. They enable immediate action in monitoring and alerting, but the pipeline must handle volume, missing packets, and clock drift before the stream becomes a trustworthy analytical table.

solo.title: Automated data collection

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Automated collection uses software and devices to capture data with minimal ongoing human effort: IoT sensors, scheduled scrapers, API pollers, and analytics platforms that emit event streams. Once configured, these systems can run continuously and feed the real-time sources discussed earlier. Automation scales and reduces some classes of human error, but it shifts cost into setup, maintenance, and privacy governance. Teams must also filter overload: a sensor that records every second can bury the rare event that matters unless retention and alerting rules are designed carefully.

solo.title: Snowball sampling

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Snowball sampling starts with a few eligible seeds and asks them to refer others who meet study criteria. The sample grows through social ties, which is often the only practical way to reach hidden or stigmatized populations when no frame exists. Referrals lower recruitment cost, yet they concentrate homogeneity: seeds recruit people like themselves. Findings should be interpreted as network-conditioned evidence rather than as population parameters, and privacy protections for both participants and referrals are essential.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova

Prevention begins at the instrument: validation rules at entry, required fields where appropriate, unique keys that prevent double posting, and documented catch-up processes when paper or offline fallbacks are used. After collection, imputation cannot invent information that was never measured.

solo.title: Dealing with bias

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Bias enters when some people or events are systematically more likely to be observed than others. At collection time the usual paths are sampling bias from uneven frames or convenience designs, selection bias when channels exclude offline populations, and measurement bias when instruments are poorly calibrated. Countermeasures are design-level: prefer random or stratified draws when inference is the goal, document exclusions, audit instruments, and report limitations transparently.
